questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: A well-functioning but a different country in terms of culture, nature etc. Moreover, a country with a different approach to academia.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The staff at Ritsumeikan is excellent at providing the students with relevant information. Almost to an extreme degree. They make checklists for exchange students to adapt to the Japanese bureaucracy regarding residence status, bank account, health insurance etc. They also provide information about housing opportunities and general matters regarding the academic life, important deadlines and courses of action as an exchange student.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The SKP staff provided help and assistance with almost every matter. My landlord was also a great help and took me to the bank and helped my to understand and fill out important paperwork in Japanese.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Ritsumeikan University has different partnerships with local landlords and has three dormitories around town. During the application process, you had to rank your desired housing form. To my understanding, Ritsumeikan is able to provide housing for all their exchange students.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is not possible to live on campus at Kinugasa Campus. You live in the northern part of Kyoto and are dependent on buses if you want to go downtown. Most housing opportunities provided by Ritsumeikan are in the proximity of Kinugasa and you will be able to walk. I lived in a private one-person apartment which was great. I know other students who have had a great time living in the dormitories as well.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You could apply for courses after the second application round. Upon arrival the registration results got published and it was possible to make changes though a second application round.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can visit the SKP staff if you have questions about the application process.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the courses I applied for, even though I had to do a second application because I had to make changes to my registration as the meritkontor, didn't accept some of my courses. If you have to make changes you can always go to the SKP staff, they will tell you what courses a still available.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
If you study at SAMF - language courses will not be accepted by the meritkontor. I had to make changes to my course registration because of this. 
Apply for as many courses as possible, this makes your prior approval (forhåndsgodkendelse) way easier, as you don't have to apply through KU's slow bureaucracy once again. You can always cancel your registration at Ritsumeikan within a reasonable time. 
    
The credit conversion is a bit confusing so make sure to get a lower credit threshold from the meritkontor, so you can stay above that.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Below average compared to KU. In Japan attendance is a part of the grading. Attendance (as in being there physically) weighs quite high on your grading.   
Most of the courses are introductory to the subject and do not go in-depth as much as I desired (the courses are only 2 credits = 4 ects). 
You will be able to follow along with ease as long as you show up and contribute to the class.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Around the same style as on KU. Some of the courses were more old school, that is an old Japanese professor talking for 1,5 hours straight. 
However, most of my courses had group work and small seminars.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Policy Case Reading 1
Public Diplomacy 
Global Political History 
Global Peace Studies 
South-East Asian Studies 
Qualitative Research Methodology 
European Studies 
Japanese Ⅰ-1(Comprehensive)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I can recommend Public Diplomacy and Global Peace Studies. The professors were engaging and had a good academic approach. 
I can also recommend Japanese Ⅰ-1(Comprehensive). It was fun to learn a new language it is also helpful if you want to function in the Japanese society.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: You have to pay for some different campus-related insurances and the mandatory student Co-op. You also have to pay for national health insurance, this is mandatory for all persons in Japan with residence status.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Food, beverages etc. are in general less expensive, and the local bus is as well.  
The Shinkansen and other JR-operated trains are quite expensive. And you can not get the tourist discount with your residence status.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Hiking, Pottery, Archery, Rugby, Rudo, Karate, Goshuin club you name it.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The pottery club is awesome and the members are really friendly. Club activities are in general the best place to meet Japanese students as you will be taking your courses with "the English speakers".

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Kyoto has a lot of nearby attractions. Mount Hiei and other mountain shrines are great to visit. You can take one-day trips to Osaka, Kobe, Himeji and Nara and weekend trips to Tokyo, Hiroshima etc.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The Japanese culture is really different and a lot of European norms are frowned upon (being loud in public, eye contact with strangers etc.). However, the Japanese understand that Westerners are different and is willing to help you in almost every situation.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: The campus clubs.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: THe language barrier. If you don't understand Japanese some things can be difficult (the ward office etc). Google translate can get you a long way. No cultural difference was challenging to an extent that something became impossible.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openness and willingness to help.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Be open-minded to the differences; experience Japan and remember to enjoy it while you can.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
It is worth the paperwork. Don't stress too much about academic matters. 
And regarding the finals. Most courses have written exams and you will not get days off for writing them.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Being able to cement yourself in a completely different setting.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The finals. Working on seven different written exams in 1,5 months was quite a challenge.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
